title: Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs Rewayat Ali Khan on 4 July, 2025
full_text: Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs Rewayat Ali Khan on 4 July, 2025 IN THE COURT OF MS. SHREYA SINGH, JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE FIRST CLASS (NI ACT) DIGITAL COURT-08, SOUTH-WEST, DWARKA COURTS, DELHI In the matter of : CC No. 6224/2017 CNR No. : DLCT020100792017 SH. RAKESH KUMAR MITTAL S/o Late Sh. Madan Lal R/o D-91, Kaushambi, Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh ...COMPLAINANT VERSUS REWAYAT ALI KHAN R/o B-47/A, IIIrd Floor, Gali No.4, Joshi Colony, Mandawali Fazalpur, Delhi-110092 ...ACCUSED JUDGMENT 1. Date of institution of the case : 26.04.2017 2. Offence complained of : Section 138 N.I. Act 3. Plea of the accused : Accused pleaded not guilty 4. Judgment reserved on : 23.05.2025 5. Decision qua accused : Convicted 6. Date of Judgment : 04.07.2025 Digitally signed by SHREYA SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.1/17 16:28:20 +0530 1. Vide this judgment, I shall decide the present complaint filed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as 'the NI Act ) by the complainant against the accused for dishonour of cheque bearing no. 103480 dated 20.03.2017 for a sum of Rs. 1,50,000/- drawn on Allahabad Bank, Pankaj Corner Plaza, Plot No.4, Mandawali Fazalpur, I.P. Extn., Patparganj, Delhi-110092 (hereinafter referred to as 'the cheque'). 2. Brief facts of the case as per complaint are that in November, 2015, the accused approached the complainant for friendly loan of Rs. 1,50,000/- as the accused was facing acute financial crisis in his business. It is averred that the complainant advanced friendly loan of Rs. 1,50,000/- to the accused for a period of three months. For availing the said loan, the accused executed a promissory note cum receipt in favour of the complainant on 01.12.2015. After expiry of three months, the complainant demanded repayment of the said loan. However, the accused avoided to make the repayment on one pretext or other. Finally, the accused issued the cheque in question towards discharge of his liability with the assurance that the same shall be honoured. Upon presentation, the cheque in question returned unpaid with remarks "Funds Insufficient" vide return memo dated 22.03.2017. It is further averred that on 05.04.2017 the complainant issued legal demand notice to the accused through speed post and the same was duly served upon the accused. Despite service of legal notice, the accused failed to pay the cheque amount within stipulated period of 15 days. Hence, the present complaint was filed. 3. The complainant led pre-summoning evidence by way of affidavit Ex. CW1/1 and on finding prima facie case, the accused was summoned vide order dated 03.07.2017. Digitally signed by SHREYA SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.2/17 2025.07.04 16:30:33 +0530 4. On appearance, the accused was served with the notice of accusation under Section 251 of Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter referred to as Cr.P.C ), to which the accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. In his defence recorded on the same day, the accused stated that he knows the complainant as they were engaged in property transactions. The accused admitted his signature on the cheque, however denied filling any other particulars. The accused further stated that "I have received legal notice from the complainant. I have furnished reply to the same." He further stated that "I had taken a loan of Rs. 1 lakh from the wife of the complainant. I had furnished the cheque in question as security cheque to the wife of the complainant. I have already made payment of Rs. 1 lakh to the wife of complainant towards a property purchased by them from one Farhatul Zehra Zaidi. Hence, I do not have any further liability towards the complainant or his wife. The complainant did not give back my security cheque despite repeated request from me." He further stated that "I have no liability." 5. The complainant examined himself as CW1 and adopted his pre- summoning evidence affidavit in post-summoning which is Ex. CW1/1 and relied upon following documents: Ex. CW1/A - Promissory note cum receipt Ex. CW1/B - Original cheque bearing no. 103480 Ex. CW1/C - Deposit slip Ex. CW1/D - Cheque return memo dated 22.03.2017 Ex. CW1/E - Legal demand notice Ex. CW1/F (Colly) - Postal receipts Ex. CW1/G (Colly) - Tracking reports Ex. CW1/H - Complaint under Section 138 NI of the Act 6. On 22.07.2019, an oral request for cross-examination of the complainant was made on behalf of the accused. Considering the plea of defence taken Digitally signed by SHREYA CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.3/17 SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:30:44 +0530 by the accused, an opportunity to cross-examine the complainant was given to the accused under Section 145(2) of the NI Act. The complainant was duly cross-examined by counsel for the accused and discharged on 07.08.2023. At request of Ld. Counsel for the complainant, complainant evidence was closed. 7. On 16.01.2024, statement of accused under Section 313 of Cr.P.C was recorded and all the incriminating evidence was put to the accused, and he was granted an opportunity to explain the circumstances appearing against him at trial. While explaining the circumstances appearing in evidence against him, the accused stated without oath that the cheque bears his sig- nature and that he did not fill any other particulars on the cheque. The ac- cused further stated that he had not received the legal notice and that the address on the legal notice is incorrect. He further stated that "Signature on the promissory note Ex. CW1/A is mine. However, it is incorrect that I had taken friendly loan of Rs. 1,50,000/- from the complainant." On being asked, whether the accused wants to lead defence evidence, the accused answered in the affirmative. 8. As per order dated 16.01.2024, the accused was given opportunity to file application under Section 315 of Cr.P.C and list of witness, if any. How- ever, despite several opportunities, the accused failed to lead defence evi- dence. Therefore, vide order dated 03.09.2024, the right of the accused to lead defence evidence was closed. Thereafter, the matter was listed for fi- nal arguments on 03.10.2024. 9. During final arguments, Ld. Counsel for complainant argued that signature on the cheque is admitted by the accused and hence, presumption is raised under Section 139 of NI Act in his favour. It is further argued that accused Digitally signed by SHREYA CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.4/17 SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:30:53 +0530 has not rebutted the presumptions raised under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act and therefore, prayed for conviction. 10. Per contra, Ld. Counsel for accused argued that is that in the accused had taken a loan of Rs. 1,50,000/- through cheques bearing no. 058132 and 058133 of Rs. 50,000/- each and Rs. 50,000/- in cash from wife of the complainant. It is further argued that the accused had issued the cheque in question to wife of the complainant as security for the said loan. It is further argued that the accused had given the cheques bearing no. 058132 and 058133 for payment, on behalf of the complainant, for purchase of property from one Farhat Ul Zehra Zaidi. It is further argued that the case of the complainant is not sufficient to prove the guilt of the accused and therefore, the accused deserves to be acquitted under Section 138 of the NI Act. In addition to oral submissions, Ld. Counsel for the accused has filed written submissions on behalf of accused and the same is part of record. 11. I have heard arguments on behalf of both the parties, perused the record, and have considered the issue at hand. 12. The ingredients of offence under Section 138 NI Act have been summarized by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Gimpex Private Limited vs. Manoj Goel MANU/SC/0829/2021 , which reads as below: "25. The ingredients of the offence under Section 138 are: (i) The drawing of a cheque by person on an account maintained by him with the banker for the payment of any amount of money to another from that account; (ii) The cheque being drawn for the discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability; (iii) Presentation of the cheque to the bank; (iv) The return of the cheque by the drawee bank as unpaid either because the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account; Digitally signed by SHREYA CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.5/17 SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:31:02 +0530 (v) A notice by the payee or the holder in due course making a demand for the payment of the amount to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information from the bank in regard to the return of the cheque; and (vi) The drawer of the cheque failing to make payment of the amount of money to the payee or the holder in due course within 15 days of the receipt of the notice." 13. The above-mentioned ingredients are to be satisfied cumulatively. Under Section 138 of the NI Act, the drawer of cheque can be held guilty only if all the above-mentioned ingredients are fulfilled. 14. In the present case, the cheque which is Ex. CW1/B is said to have been issued by the accused, and it is said to bear signature of the accused. The cheque return memo dated 22.03.2017 which is Ex. CW1/D provides the reason for dishonour as 'Funds Insufficient'. The line of cross-examination adopted by the accused for CW1 does not in any manner dispute the signature of the accused on Ex. CW1/B. This is perhaps for the reason that the accused, both at the stage of framing of notice under Section 251 of Cr.P.C and recording of statement of accused under Section 313 of Cr.P.C, has stated that the signature found on the cheque Ex. CW1/B is his own signature. Further, the cheque is dated 20.03.2017 and the same was returned vide return memo dated 22.03.2017, which proves that the cheque was presented within the period of validity. As per Section 146 of the NI Act, the fact of dishonour of cheque is presumed upon production of bank's slip having the official mark denoting that the cheque in question has been dishonoured. A presumption is raised in favour of complainant as the cheque in question was dishonoured vide return memo dated 22.03.2017 which is Ex. CW1/D. 15. As regards making demand of payment of the cheque amount in writing, the complainant sent legal demand notice which is Ex. CW1/E to the Digitally signed by SHREYA CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.6/17 SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:31:12 +0530 accused. The original postal receipts which are Ex. CW1/F (Colly) are dated 05.04.2017. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed and is evident from a bare reading of the legal demand notice. 16. Ld. Counsel for accused has argued that the accused had not received the legal notice from the complainant as the same was sent on a wrong / incorrect address. It is further argued that during framing of notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C., the accused mistook summons of the court to be legal notice sent by the complainant and admitted service of legal notice. Ld. Counsel for accused has placed reliance on R. L. Varma & Sons (HUF) vs. P.C. Sharma MANU/DE/2040/2019 , Kishore vs. Arul Jothi (2017(3) MWN (Cr.) DCC 29 (Mad.) and Mr. Rama Chandra Panigrahi vs. State of Orissa & Anr. MANU/OR/0047/2003 in support of his submissions. 17. It is pertinent to note that there is an inconsistency in the stand of the accused. On the one hand, the accused accepted receipt of legal notice and claimed he had issued a reply during his plea, but on the other hand, he claimed that the address was incorrect during recording of his statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C. The court is not convinced by the argument that the accused mistook legal notice as summons from this Court as he specifically claimed that he issued a reply as well. For this reason alone, the argument that there was some confusion in the mind of the accused deserves to be rejected. In any event, neither statements have any evidentiary value as they are not on oath. Hence, this court is required to assess the other material available on record. 18. The complainant has specifically averred in the complaint that the legal demand notice was issued to the accused by speed post and the same was Digitally signed by SHREYA SHREYA SINGH CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.7/17 SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:31:25 +0530 duly served to the accused. The original postal receipts, Ex. CW1/F (Colly) bear the name and part of addresses of the accused. Therefore, the complainant is entitled to presumption under Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 read with Section 114 of the IEA as held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji vs. Palapetty Muhammed and Ors. MANU/SC/2263/2007 . In addition, the Hon'ble Supreme Court also held that when the notice is sent by registered post by correctly addressing the drawer of the cheque, the mandatory requirement of issuance of notice in terms of clause (b) of proviso to Section 138 of the Act stands complied with. 19. In addition to the above presumption, the address in the complaint and the address to which the legal notice is issued are the same. The summons issued to accused in the present complaint returned back with remark 'refused'. The accused has appeared before this court after issuance of non- bailable warrants on the same address as shown in legal notice. In the case of Manoj Jain vs. Surinder Kumar Jain & Anr. MANU/DE/1981/2015 , the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi observed that: "14. The assertion of the Petitioner that the demand notice was not received by him as it was sent on a wrong address. The summons by the court which were also sent at the same address, were received by him. The notice, which was sent by UPC did not return, indicating that it was served. Thus, both the courts below rightly held that notice was validly served." 20. The appearance of accused on the basis of issuance of process of the court on the same address as mentioned in the legal notice does not support the argument of the accused that the legal notice was sent to wrong address. Even the tracking reports which are Ex. CW1/G (Colly) show that the legal demand notice was delivered to the accused. Moreover, in reply to notice framed under Section 251 Cr.P.C, the accused stated that he had received legal notice from the complainant, and he had furnished reply to the same. Digitally signed by SHREYA CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.8/17 SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:31:35 +0530 21. Further, the judgments sought to be relied upon by Ld. Counsel for the accused are all on the facts where the address was shown to be the 'wrong' address. In the present case, the accused has not shown that he had any other address or that the address in the legal notice is the wrong address. As such, it appears that these judgments which were delivered in different sets of facts and circumstances are of no assistance to defence. Accordingly, the fifth ingredient of offence under Section 138 NI Act stands fulfilled. 22. It is not in dispute that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of receipt of the legal demand notice. Therefore, I have no hesitation in holding that first, third, fourth and sixth ingredients of the offence under Section 138 of NI Act stand fulfilled. 23. Coming to the second ingredient of the offence i.e. that the drawer of the cheque should have issued the cheque for the discharge, in whole or in part, of a legally enforceable debt or other liability. It is the case of the complainant that in November, 2015 the accused had sought friendly loan of Rs. 1,50,000/- from the complainant and the same was given to the accused for a period of three months. Towards discharge of his debt and liability, the accused issued the cheque in question to the complainant. However, upon presentation, the cheque was dishonoured. 24. As illustrated above, the signature of the accused on the cheque which Ex. CW1/B is not in dispute. Hence, Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act are required to be considered at this stage. The combined effect of Sections 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act is that a presumption can be raised that the cheque was drawn for consideration and given by the accused for the discharge of legally enforceable debt or other liability. Both the Digitally signed by SHREYA CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.9/17 SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:31:44 +0530 sections use the expression "shall", which makes it imperative for the court to raise the presumptions, once the foundational facts required for the same are proved. 25. This issue is no longer res integra and has been well settled. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Hiten P. Dalal vs. Bratindranath Banerjee MANU/SC/0359/2001 has summarised this proposition as below: "23. In other words, provided the facts required to form the basis of a presumption of law exists, no discretion is left with the Court but to draw the statutory conclusion, but this does not preclude the person against whom the presumption is drawn from rebutting it and proving the contrary. A fact is said to be proved when, "after considering the matters before it, the Court either believes it to exist, or considers its existence so probable that a prudent man ought, under the circumstances of the particular case, to act upon the supposition that it exists". Therefore, the rebuttal does not have to be conclusively established but such evidence must be adduced before the Court in support of the defence that the Court must either believe the defence to exist or consider its existence to be reasonably probable, the standard of reasonability being that of the 'prudent man'." 26. Thus, it is clear that once the execution of cheque is established, the law raises presumption in favour of payee or holder of cheque that the cheque was issued in discharge, wholly or in part, of legally enforceable debt or liability. The legal effect of the presumption raised is that the onus now shifts on the accused to raise a probable defence to rebut the statutory presumption. The manner in which an accused can rebut this presumption has been summarized by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Basalingappa vs. Mudibasappa MANU/SC/0502/2019 as under: "23. We having noticed the ratio laid down by this Court in above cases on Sections 118(a) and 139 , we now summarise the principles enumerated by this Court in following manner: (i) Once the execution of cheque is admitted Section 139 of the Act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. Digitally signed by SHREYA CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.10/17 SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:31:52 +0530 (ii) The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. (iii) To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. (iv) That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence, Section 139 imposed an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. (v) It is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box to support his defence." (emphasis supplied) 27. The accused may choose to rebut the presumption by relying on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. The standard of proof to rebut the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. 28. In view of the above stated law, the admission of the accused regarding signature on the cheque in question, the statutory presumption is bound to be raised in terms of Sections 118 (a) and 139 of the NI Act that the cheque in question was issued in discharge of, whole or in part of, legally enforceable debt or liability. 29. Once the statutory presumption is raised in favour of the complainant, the burden of proof now lies upon the accused to rebut the statutory presumption by raising probable defence either by leading defence evidence or by bringing out such facts on record in the cross-examination of the complainant that could make the complainant's case improbable. If Digitally signed by CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.11/17 SHREYA SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:32:01 +0530 the accused is able to discharge his burden by raising probable defence, then and only then the onus will again shift back upon the complainant. 30. The accused has chosen not to enter the witness box himself and adduce any oral or documentary evidence of his own. The only material available for this Court to determine the guilt/innocence of the accused are the evidence affidavit and documents produced by CW1 and the cross- examination of CW1 conducted by the accused. 31. The defence of accused as stated in the written submission filed on behalf of the accused is that in October, 2013, the accused had taken loan of Rs. 1,50,000/- through cheques bearing no. 058132 and 058133 of Rs. 50,000/- each and Rs. 50,000/- in cash from wife of the complainant; that he had issued the cheque in question and a blank signed promissory note to wife of the complainant as security for the said loan; that the complainant agreed to buy a property from one Farhat Ul Zehra Zaidi; that as per agreement to sell with Farhat Ul Zehra Zaidi hse was required to make advance payment of Rs. 3,00,000/-; that due to shortage of Rs. 1,00,000/-, the complainant requested the accused to return the said cheques to him; that after return of the said cheques, the said cheques were given to Farhat Ul Zehra Zaidi for making advance payment; that the said cheques were issued in the name of the accused, the same were encashed by the accused on the assurance that Rs. 1,00,000/- will be given to him within one week; that wife of the complainant did not make payment of Rs. 1,00,000/- to the accused and in fact, demanded back Rs. 50,000/- paid to him in cash; that wife of the complainant assured that she will return the cheque in question and blank signed promissory note to the accused upon completion of sale transaction between the complainant and Farhat Ul Zehra Zaidi; that deal of purchase of property was cancelled and Farhat Ul Zehra Zaidi did not Digitally signed by SHREYA SHREYA SINGH CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.12/17 SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:32:10 +0530 return the earnest money of Rs. 3,00,000/- to the complainant. Consequently, wife of the complainant did not to return the cheque in question and blank signed promissory note to the accused. 32. During cross-examination, CW1 admitted that he had entered into a written agreement dated 25.10.2013 with Farhat Ul Zehra Zaidi for purchase of property for a sum of Rs. 14,15,000/-. CW1 further admitted that he had given Rs. 3 Lakhs to Farhat Ul Zehra Zaidi as advance for purchase of property. CW1 further admitted that transaction dated 25.10.2013 did not mature as Farhat Ul Zehra Zaidi sold the property to someone else. CW1 stated that Farhat Ul Zehra Zaidi did not return the advance payment of Rs. 3 Lakhs given by him at the time of execution of agreement dated 25.10.2013. However, these statements do not help the defence of the accused as the accused has not been able to demonstrate any direct connection between the transaction with Farhat Ul Zehra Zaidi and his liability to repay the complainant. CW1 denied the suggestion put to him that in October, 2013 his wife had given loan of Rs. 1,50,000/- through cheques bearing no. 058132 and 058133 of Rs. 50,000/- each and Rs. 50,000/- in cash to the accused. CW1 also denied the suggestion that his wife received blank signed promissory note and cheque in question as security for loan of Rs. 1,50,000/- from the accused. 33. It is pertinent to note that the accused has not adduced any documentary or oral evidence to prove his version that he had taken a loan of Rs. 1,50,000/- from wife of the complainant and that he had issued blank signed promissory note along with the cheque in question as security for the same. During final arguments, Ld. Counsel for the accused has relied upon certified copy of plaint filed by the complainant and his wife against Farhat Ul Zehra Zaidi and the accused and the testimony of PW1 recorded Digitally signed by SHREYA CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.13/17 SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:32:19 +0530 in suit for recovery of Rs. 7,47,054/- pending before the court of Ld. District Judge, Karkardooma Court. The certified copy produced on behalf of the accused cannot be looked into by this court for the very reason that the same was not led in evidence by the accused. Pleadings between parties in different forums, if relevant, should form part of evidence. However, the same ought to have been produced at the appropriate stage to enable cross- examination by the opposite party. To look at the plaint now when the accused has chosen not to either confront it to CW1 or produce it as part of his own defence, would mean a clear violation of the fair procedure. Further, the complainant will be deprived of an opportunity to explain the circumstances or conduct cross-examination on the documents produced by the accused. Hence, the court is not inclined to examine the documents produced on behalf of accused at the stage of final arguments. 34. In any event, the suit in relation to which the plaint has now been produced is currently pending adjudication. The accused has not been able to show that his liability has been either accepted or rejected by the Ld. District Judge. The present case stands on a different footing from the said civil suit. In that light, the reliance of the accused on the plaint and the testimony of PW1 in that case is misplaced and does not assist his case. 35. In order to prove the liability of the accused, the complainant has adduced original promissory note cum receipt which is Ex. CW1/A. In the statement recorded under Section 313 Cr.P.C, the accused stated that Ex. CW1/A bears his signature. The signature on Ex. CW1/A is not disputed by the accused. The accused has only disputed the issuance of the promissory note to the complainant. It is the version of the accused that he had issued blank signed promissory note to wife of the complainant. Nothing is elicited in the cross-examination to prove this version of the Digitally signed by SHREYA CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.14/17 SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:32:28 +0530 accused. On the one hand, the complainant has produced documentary evidence in the form of promissory note and cheque which is Ex. CW1/A, whereas the accused has relied only on his narrative that the cheque was issued to wife of the complainant. The accused claims that payments made to him by wife of the complainant in part through cheque have been returned. The accused has not produced evidence of the alleged transaction with the wife. Hence, no probable reason is provided by the accused for singing a blank promissory note. 36. During cross-examination of CW1, certain questions on the aspect of financial capacity and filing of ITR were put on behalf of the accused. On this aspect, CW1 deposed that in 2015 he was running a hotel in Karol Bagh, New Delhi, however he does not remember his annual income from hotel in 2015. CW1 further deposed that in 2015 he was income tax payee, but he does not remember whether he had filed ITR in 2015 or not. 37. Before proceeding to decide the question whether the complainant had financial capacity to advance loan of Rs. 1,50,000/- to the accused, it is important to note the settled position of law regarding financial capacity. In the case of Tedhi Singh vs. Narayan Dass Mahant MANU/SC/0310/2022 , the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that the complainant does not have initial burden to lead evidence to prove his financial capacity. However, the accused has right to demonstrate that the complainant lacked financial capacity to advance the loan in question. If the accused raises a legitimate defence based on financial capacity, then the burden would turn on the complainant to prove his financial capacity based on cogent evidence. 38. In the cross-examination of CW1, nothing is elicited to disbelieve the version of the complainant in relation to the loan transaction. The accused Digitally signed by SHREYA CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.15/17 SHREYA SINGH SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:32:38 +0530 specifically suggests that after entering into an agreement, CW1 had made an advance payment of at least Rs. 2,00,000 to another third party for purchase of a property. Such being the case, the accused has not shown any material to doubt the financial capacity of the complainant. When the accused admits that CW1 had capacity to have made advance payment of Rs. 2,00,000 by introducing these facts during cross-examination, the mere non-filing of ITR in the present case would not lead to conclusion that the complainant had no capacity to advance loan of Rs. 1,50,000. On a balance of probabilities, this court is not persuaded that the loan transaction did not take place as claimed by the accused or that there was a parallel transaction only with the wife of the accused. The accused has not been able to issue narrative for the issuance of promissory note and the cheque. Hence, there is no probable defence. 39. Accordingly, the complainant has been able to prove all the ingredients of the offence under Section 138 of the NI Act and there is no probable defence raised and established by the accused. It is evident that the complainant has been able to prove that the cheque in question i.e. cheque bearing no. 103480 dated 20.03.2017 for a sum of Rs. 1,50,000/- drawn on Allahabad Bank, Pankaj Corner Plaza, Plot No.4, Mandawali Fazalpur, I.P. Extn., Patparganj, Delhi-110092 which is Ex. CW1/B was issued in discharge of legally recoverable liability owed by the accused towards the complainant. 40. In view of the above, this court has arrived at a finding that the accused is guilty of offence under Section 138 of the NI Act. Accordingly, accused Rewayat Ali Khan is hereby convicted under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 41. Let the convict be heard on quantum of sentence. Digitally signed by SHREYA SHREYA SINGH CC No. 6224/2017 Rakesh Kumar Mittal vs. Rewayat Ali Khan Page No.16/17 SINGH Date: 2025.07.04 16:32:47 +0530 42. Copy of Judgment be supplied to the convict free of cost.
